proposal.answer: Plan A costs $120/month with a 10-second recovery checkpoint and a capacity of 40 concurrent requests, while Plan B costs $75/month with a 30-second recovery checkpoint and a capacity of 24 concurrent requests. Evidence from stress test trials indicates that Plan A consistently handles higher loads with lower latency; for instance, at 25 active requests (Trial 17), Plan A maintained a p95 latency of 408 ms and completed all requests, whereas Plan B saturated, failing to complete requests beyond its declared capacity with a p95 latency of 507 ms. The tradeoff is clear: Plan B offers a lower monthly cost ($45 savings) but sacrifices capacity, recovery frequency (slower checkpoints), and performance stability under load. As noted in the product trial conclusion, 'lower monthly cost alone does not establish superior user response latency,' meaning the cheaper Plan B may result in poorer user experience during peak usage due to saturation and higher latency.

sections.text: Plan A is significantly more expensive at $120 per month compared to Plan B at $75 per month. However, this cost difference buys higher resource allocation and performance guarantees.

Plan A offers faster recovery with checkpoints every 10 seconds versus every 30 seconds for Plan B. Capacity-wise, Plan A supports 40 concurrent requests using 800 MB RAM, while Plan B supports only 24 concurrent requests using 500 MB RAM.

Stress tests show Plan B saturates above 24 concurrent requests (e.g., Trial 17), leading to incomplete request processing and higher latency (p95 > 500ms). Plan A remains stable up to its 40-request limit with lower latency. The tradeoff is cost versus reliability and throughput; choosing Plan B saves money but risks service degradation under moderate load.
